rv.q: This extraordinary show is absolutely, extremely and very deliberately contrived: a slippery, shape-shifting duet that keeps changing the rules of engagement — with the material, with the premise, with the audience.
Crouch performs a magic trick: transforming their real discomfort into the crackling tension between two characters bound together by grief and guilt.
Yet tonight it does feel more contrived than revelatory.
Yet the incontrovertible fact is that these 75 minutes of drama are a little too pleased with themselves – more pleased than we spectators will ever manage to be.
The parallels between an actor lost on stage and a man lost in mourning are just one of the play’s many masterstrokes.
Despite the premise oozing potential, what may have seemed novel 20 years ago, now looks a little half-baked, even embarrassing in places.

cn.t: Critics are split on An Oak Tree's 20th anniversary run. Most praise its shape-shifting theatricality and emotional power, while skeptics find the celebrity-guest conceit more novelty than substance.
